Overview

What Volt Streaming is

Volt Streaming is a complete, multi-tenant platform for running live television channels, live events, radio stations and the on-demand content that flows out of them. It was designed and built during 2026 as a clean-sheet product: a new codebase, a new data model and a new operator console, with no lineage from any earlier system. It draws on more than a decade of building and operating streaming platforms for broadcasters, and it is deliberately shaped around the workflows those operators actually run every day.

The platform is live-first. A channel, an event and a radio station are all treated as one kind of thing, a stream, that shares the same pipeline for ingest, encoding, packaging, delivery, recording, monitoring and analytics. Everything that happens on air is captured, and anything captured can be found, clipped, reviewed and published within minutes. The reverse direction, turning a library of assets into a scheduled linear channel, is designed into the same model.

Why it was built

Most platforms in this space were built for one workflow and had others bolted on. The result is familiar to any operator: bespoke deployment for every new client, reporting that never quite reconciles, and add-ons nobody wants to touch. Volt starts from the opposite position. One product, one data model, provisioning that is automated rather than hand-built, and reporting that comes from measured facts rather than estimates.

Who it is for

Broadcasters and network operators who run several live outputs at once, need a defensible record of what went to air, and want to turn live output into on-demand content without a separate production step. It is equally suited to a single broadcaster and to an operator hosting many tenants on one deployment.

Design foundations

Built to stay simple as it grows

A handful of decisions were made early and hold everywhere in the product. They are the reason new capability can be added as configuration rather than as new code paths, and the reason the platform is straightforward to operate at scale.

One stream spine

Channels, events, radio stations and future scheduled-playout channels are presets of a single stream model, not separate silos. Delivery, monitoring, recording, listing and analytics are shared. Adding a new kind of output is additive configuration.

Live and on-demand are symmetrical

Metadata, output description and publishing rules are defined once and travel with the content. A live event that ends becomes an on-demand asset with the same description, and a library of assets can feed a linear output using the same contracts.

Production is separate from distribution

What runs the pipeline (inputs, encoding profile, placement) changes rarely. What describes and publishes it (metadata, availability, destinations) changes constantly. Keeping them apart means visibility and destinations can change without touching the media path.

Multi-tenant from the first line

Every record belongs to an account, every request is scoped to one, and isolation is tested. Parent and child accounts, platform-level roles and per-tenant limits are built in rather than layered on. One deployment can host many broadcasters.

Health you can read in one glance

Every stream reports five gates in order: server, input, encoder, output and on air. A fault shows where the chain broke. The same model drives automatic reconnection, the monitoring page and the quality-check “what went wrong” diagnosis.

Facts, not estimates

Hours on air, listener egress, peak concurrency and audience are measured at the point they happen and stored as ledgers. Reports either return a real figure or say honestly that one is not retained. There is no “roughly”.

Every change is accountable

Edits are partial, versioned and audited: who changed what, from what, to what. Two operators editing the same record are warned about each other. Deletes of anything in use are guarded.

Standards over invention

HLS, DASH and CMAF for delivery. SRT, RTMP, HLS and Icecast in. schema.org and JSON-LD for descriptions and the API. WebVTT for captions. Standard formats mean standard players, standard CDNs and no lock-in for the customer.

Runs anywhere. The whole platform, encoder included, runs on a single laptop for development and evaluation, and deploys to a cloud stack defined entirely as infrastructure-as-code. Local and cloud share one codebase; the storage and launch layers are swappable drivers.

Capabilities

Live, radio, recording and clipping

Live channels and events

  • Transcode workflow (full adaptive-bitrate ladder built by the platform) or package-only workflow (take a pre-encoded ladder and package it), per channel.
  • Common output: CMAF segments served as HLS and DASH, with a per-channel DVR window of up to four hours in sliding or event-start mode.
  • Input failover with automatic filler on source loss; slates and loops as managed filler assets.
  • Watermark and channel bug burn-in with live preview; brand image, colour and description carried to guide clients.
  • Multi-language audio tracks detected from the source and offered in the player with a track picker.
  • Events have a bounded public window, a separate “encoder running” and “output public” state, and scheduled clips that fire on the timeline and produce on-demand assets automatically when the event ends.
  • Geo and rights rules per stream and per programme: blackouts by country with a replacement asset served to blocked viewers.

Radio and audio

  • Audio-only stations with Icecast or HLS in, and MP3, HLS and DASH out from one encode; no video ladder, no GPU.
  • Now-playing metadata captured as a timed log for every station, searchable and clippable by title; sensible fallbacks for sources that carry no metadata.
  • Real level metering and audio-present checks measured from the broadcast output, not the source.
  • Whole-audience listener counts across MP3 and player clients, and per-listener measured egress for cost and pricing.

Recording and clipping

  • Continuous recording of every channel, station and event, with retention policy and broadcast-day roll-over.
  • A source timeline showing what was recorded, what was on air and where the gaps are, across the whole retained range; zoom from one minute to a day.
  • A clipping workbench with waveform, keyboard scrubbing, in/out marks, and frame-exact cuts across segment boundaries. Gaps inside the marks are flagged before a clip is made, not discovered afterwards.
  • Non-destructive re-trim: change the in and out points of a published clip without touching the recording.
  • Compose a clip across several recordings; export as streaming manifest, MP4, MP3 or AAC.
  • Poster frames, storyboard thumbnails and scrub previews generated for every recording.

Capabilities

Publishing, guides, captions and analytics

Media library and publishing

  • Everything that has been cut, where it came from and where it went, in one library with review states, quality-check results and published status.
  • Automatic QC on every asset (coverage, playlist continuity, timing, audio level) with a plain-language diagnosis when something is wrong.
  • Metadata harvested from the event or programme flows into the asset and out as schema.org descriptions, ready for search engines and guide partners.
  • Share links for private review: expiry, PIN, view caps, email delivery and QR, rotate or revoke at any time. A channel can be shared for review before it goes on air.
  • Publishing destinations and view tracking per asset; the foundation for social publishing to YouTube, Facebook, X, TikTok and Dailymotion is in place.
  • Embeddable player with skins, an SDK and headless mode; an on-the-fly image service for posters, thumbnails and artwork at any size.

Programme guides and scheduling

  • Guides for channels, stations and events with recurring programmes, conflict and overlap detection, and copy-day tooling.
  • Each slot can control geo access, trigger a slate, loop or replacement asset, and cut a clip automatically after airing.
  • Programme boundaries are carried inside the delivery stream itself, so players and downstream systems see now/next without polling.
  • Guide export for set-top and app partners (channel list with icons, colours and descriptions).

Captions and translation

  • Live transcription and subtitles per stream, aligned to the media timeline and proven in a real player, with a self-hosted engine (no per-minute cost) or a paid cloud engine, chosen per account.
  • Translation into further languages in the same pass. English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil pairs have been exercised end to end.

Analytics and reporting

  • Server-side audience measurement from delivery logs: views, unique viewers, watch hours, peak concurrent, by device, country and app. No client SDK required, so it cannot be blocked by an ad-blocker or a VPN.
  • Daily roll-ups keep answering after raw events age out; real-time “watching now” for live outputs.
  • Ledgers for hours on air and measured listener egress make per-tenant and per-station cost answerable for pricing and billing.

Capabilities

Operations and platform management

Operating the fleet

  • A dashboard that answers three questions: is anything broken, what is on air, and what is waiting on me.
  • A monitoring page that shows problems only. A healthy fleet leaves it empty, which is the point.
  • Fleet activity collapses repeated events into one row rather than a wall of identical lines.
  • Automatic reconnection that arms itself only after a stream has proven healthy, so a mis-configured first start is left where it fell with its reason intact instead of being retried into oblivion.
  • Per-stream event log, give-up notices and log clearing, each audited.
  • Multiview for watching several outputs at once; site-wide search across channels, stations, events and recordings.
  • Fleet and usage view: encoders, relays and storage with indicative cost per tenant.

API and integration

  • A complete REST API behind the console, with typed links and machine-readable documentation so integrators can discover it rather than read about it.
  • Public, admin and platform routes are classified and enforced; account API keys with per-app restrictions and playback tokens.
  • Notification service with templates, fan-out by recipient and channel, delivery log and retries.

Running it as a service

  • Accounts, users and roles; platform-level roles for the operator (administrator, support, read-only) with two-step login.
  • Platform dashboard across all tenants: servers, upcoming events, projected capacity, active channels, viewers, API status and open tickets.
  • Support tickets filed by clients and triaged by the operator; account “view as” for support, fully audited.
  • Per-tenant limits (for example channel count) enforced and surfaced as alerts when exceeded.
  • Image library and file manager per account: watermarks, slates, posters and brand assets, with guarded deletes.
  • Watch-folder ingest rules with a quarantine path for files that match nothing, so nothing is silently ingested or silently lost.

Provisioning. A new tenant, channel or station is created from the console and provisioned by the platform. There is no per-client hand-built deployment, and no per-client fork of the software. This is the single largest change in operating cost compared with the way most platforms in this space are run today.

Maturity

Where the build stands today

Volt Streaming is a working platform, not a concept. The figures below are counted from the codebase as of September 2026.

25
console pages in the operator application
48
API route groups behind the console
80+
automated check suites, run against real media where it matters
~50k
lines of application code across control plane, console and encoder
1 codebase
runs on a laptop and deploys to the cloud unchanged
IaC
complete cloud stack defined as infrastructure-as-code

Built and verified

Everything described on pages 4 to 6 is built and covered by automated checks unless noted otherwise. The encoder and packager have been validated against real sources, including SRT and Icecast ingest, and the caption timeline has been proven in a real browser player rather than on paper. Multi-tenant isolation, access control and the audit trail are tested end to end.

Designed, next to build

  • Scheduled playout (turn a library of assets into a linear channel) on the existing stream model.
  • HTML graphics overlays: scorebug, lower third, sponsor bug and ticker, rendered once and burned into the encode.
  • Ad markers in the delivery stream for server-side ad insertion.
  • Single sign-on with Microsoft and Google.
  • Social publishing connectors (the data model and API exist; per-platform credentials are needed).
  • Automatic guide inference for stations that hand over a URL and no schedule.

What comes with the platform

  • Full source for the control plane, operator console and encoder/packager.
  • The cloud deployment definition and local run tooling.
  • Design documents for every subsystem, requirements documents, the API reference and an integration collection.
  • The automated test base and the scripts that run it.
  • A build status board and feature tracker reconciling design decisions against what is built.

Not included in this document. Architecture detail, data model, deployment topology and pricing are deliberately left out at this stage. They are available under a suitable agreement once there is mutual interest.
